note: What each spoken step needs, in nawana's own words. `level` = the step at which the item should be solid. Grammar items are tagged right/wrong per talk; function items are tagged when the learner DID it. Vocabulary and fluency are measured in code, not here. See docs/personal-report-plan.md.

grammar.name: be: am / is / are
grammar.counts: any form of present 'be' as main verb or in a basic sentence
grammar.example: I'm tired. She is a nurse.
grammar.error: I tired. She a nurse.

grammar.name: present simple, including he/she/it -s
grammar.counts: habits, facts, states with a present-simple main verb
grammar.example: She works in Berlin.
grammar.error: She work in Berlin.

grammar.name: basic questions with do / be
grammar.counts: a yes/no or wh- question the learner forms
grammar.example: Where do you live? Is it far?
grammar.error: Where you live? It is far?

grammar.name: negatives with don't / doesn't / not
grammar.counts: a negative present sentence
grammar.example: He doesn't like coffee.
grammar.error: He no like coffee. He don't like coffee.

grammar.name: can / can't for ability and requests
grammar.counts: can + base verb
grammar.example: Can you help me? I can't swim.
grammar.error: I can to swim. Can you to help?

grammar.name: there is / there are
grammar.counts: existence sentences
grammar.example: There are two parks near my house.
grammar.error: Have two parks near my house. There is two parks.

grammar.name: a / an / the
grammar.counts: a singular countable noun that needs an article
grammar.example: I bought a new phone. The screen is big.
grammar.error: I bought new phone. Screen is big.

grammar.name: plurals and possessives (my, your, 's)
grammar.counts: plural nouns, possessive adjectives, 's
grammar.example: My sister's kids are five and seven.
grammar.error: My sister kid are five and seven.

grammar.name: in / on / at for time and place
grammar.counts: a time or place phrase with in/on/at
grammar.example: on Monday, at 8, in the morning, at work
grammar.error: in Monday, on 8, at the morning

grammar.name: present continuous for now
grammar.counts: am/is/are + -ing for something happening now or around now
grammar.example: I'm cooking dinner right now.
grammar.error: I cooking dinner. I am cook now.

grammar.name: past simple, regular and irregular
grammar.counts: a finished past event with a past-simple verb
grammar.example: Yesterday I went to the market and bought fish.
grammar.error: Yesterday I go to the market. I buyed fish.

grammar.name: past questions and negatives with did
grammar.counts: did/didn't + base verb
grammar.example: Did you sleep well? I didn't go.
grammar.error: Did you slept? I didn't went.

grammar.name: going to for plans
grammar.counts: be going to + base verb
grammar.example: I'm going to visit my parents.
grammar.error: I going to visit. I'm going to visiting.

grammar.name: will for predictions, offers and decisions
grammar.counts: will / won't + base verb
grammar.example: It'll rain later. I'll call you.
grammar.error: It will rains. I will to call you.

grammar.name: comparatives and superlatives
grammar.counts: -er/more ... than, the -est/most
grammar.example: Seoul is bigger than Busan. It's the best place.
grammar.error: more bigger, more big than, the most good

grammar.name: frequency adverbs (always, usually, never)
grammar.counts: a frequency adverb in a sentence
grammar.example: I usually get up at seven.
grammar.error: I get up usually at seven. Always I get up.

grammar.name: some / any / much / many / a lot of
grammar.counts: a quantifier with a noun
grammar.example: There isn't much time. I have a lot of friends.
grammar.error: many time, much friends

grammar.name: have to / must / should
grammar.counts: obligation or advice with these modals
grammar.example: You should try it. I have to work tomorrow.
grammar.error: You should to try. I must to work.

grammar.name: and / but / because / so
grammar.counts: two clauses joined with these
grammar.example: I was tired, so I went home.
grammar.error: Because I was tired. So I went home. (fragment only)

grammar.name: want to / would like to / like -ing
grammar.counts: a verb + to-infinitive or -ing after want, like, love, hate, would like
grammar.example: I'd like to try. I love cooking.
grammar.error: I want go. I like cook.

grammar.name: present continuous for arrangements
grammar.counts: am/is/are + -ing for a fixed future plan
grammar.example: I'm meeting Jin on Friday.
grammar.error: I meet Jin on Friday. (for an arrangement)

grammar.name: present perfect for experience (ever / never / before)
grammar.counts: have/has + past participle about life experience
grammar.example: Have you ever been to Japan? I've never tried it.
grammar.error: Did you ever go to Japan? I never try it.

grammar.name: present perfect with for / since
grammar.counts: have/has + participle for a state continuing to now
grammar.example: I've lived here for three years.
grammar.error: I live here for three years. I am living here since 2020.

grammar.name: past continuous (was / were -ing)
grammar.counts: an action in progress in the past, often interrupted
grammar.example: I was walking home when it started to rain.
grammar.error: I walked home when it started. I was walk home.

grammar.name: used to for past habits
grammar.counts: used to + base verb
grammar.example: I used to play the piano.
grammar.error: I used to playing. I use to play.

grammar.name: first conditional (if + present, will)
grammar.counts: a real future condition
grammar.example: If it rains, we'll stay home.
grammar.error: If it will rain, we stay home.

grammar.name: second conditional (if + past, would)
grammar.counts: an imagined present or future
grammar.example: If I had more time, I would travel.
grammar.error: If I have more time, I would travel. If I would have time...

grammar.name: defining relative clauses (who / which / that / where)
grammar.counts: a noun defined by a relative clause
grammar.example: That's the guy who fixed my bike.
grammar.error: That's the guy fixed my bike. the place which I live

grammar.name: might / may / could for possibility
grammar.counts: a modal of possibility + base verb
grammar.example: It might be closed.
grammar.error: Maybe it might be closed? It might closed.

grammar.name: present and past passive
grammar.counts: be + past participle
grammar.example: The bridge was built in 1900.
grammar.error: The bridge built in 1900. It was build.

grammar.name: reported statements (said / told me that)
grammar.counts: reporting what someone said
grammar.example: She told me she was busy.
grammar.error: She said me she is busy. She told that...

grammar.name: gerund vs infinitive after verbs
grammar.counts: verbs like enjoy, finish, avoid, decide, plan, stop, remember + -ing/to
grammar.example: I enjoy cooking. I decided to quit.
grammar.error: I enjoy to cook. I decided quitting.

grammar.name: time and contrast clauses (when, while, although, even though)
grammar.counts: a subordinate clause with these
grammar.example: Although it was late, we kept talking.
grammar.error: Although it was late, but we kept talking.

grammar.name: present perfect continuous
grammar.counts: have been + -ing for an activity up to now
grammar.example: I've been studying all morning.
grammar.error: I'm studying since morning. I have studying.

grammar.name: past perfect (had + participle)
grammar.counts: an earlier past before another past
grammar.example: When I arrived, they had already left.
grammar.error: When I arrived, they already left. (when sequence matters)

grammar.name: third conditional (if + had, would have)
grammar.counts: an imagined past
grammar.example: If I had known, I would have come.
grammar.error: If I knew, I would come. If I would have known...

grammar.name: should have / could have / must have
grammar.counts: modal + have + participle
grammar.example: I should have called you. He must have forgotten.
grammar.error: I should called you. He must forgot.

grammar.name: passive with modals and perfect; have something done
grammar.counts: can be done, has been done, get/have something done
grammar.example: It has to be finished today. I had my hair cut.
grammar.error: It has to finish today. I cut my hair. (at the hairdresser)

grammar.name: non-defining relative clauses
grammar.counts: extra information with , who / , which
grammar.example: My boss, who is usually calm, was furious.
grammar.error: My boss that is usually calm...

grammar.name: reported questions
grammar.counts: asked if / asked where with statement word order
grammar.example: She asked me where I lived.
grammar.error: She asked me where do I live.

grammar.name: wish / if only
grammar.counts: wish + past or past perfect
grammar.example: I wish I had more time.
grammar.error: I wish I have more time.

grammar.name: future continuous and future perfect
grammar.counts: will be -ing, will have + participle
grammar.example: This time tomorrow I'll be flying.
grammar.error: This time tomorrow I will fly.

grammar.name: despite, whereas, unless, as long as, in case
grammar.counts: a clause or phrase with these
grammar.example: Despite the rain, we went out.
grammar.error: Despite it rained, we went out.

functions.name: introduce yourself and give simple facts
functions.counts: says who they are, where from, what they do

functions.name: say what you like and don't like
ask for and offer simple things
describe your routine and daily life
say simply what happened
functions.counts: reports a past event in one or two sentences

functions.name: talk about plans
functions.counts: says what they will do or plan to do

functions.name: give a simple opinion with a reason
tell a story in order
functions.counts: three or more events in sequence, with time words (first, then, after that)

functions.name: explain and justify a choice
functions.counts: gives a choice with more than one reason or a detailed reason

functions.name: agree or disagree politely
functions.counts: states agreement/disagreement with a view and a reason

functions.name: deal with a problem or something unexpected
functions.counts: explains a problem and asks for or proposes a solution

functions.name: keep the conversation going
functions.counts: asks the other person a follow-up question about what THEY said

functions.name: weigh options, pros and cons
functions.counts: compares two or more options with advantages/disadvantages

functions.name: speculate about what could be or could have been
develop an argument with supporting points
functions.counts: a view supported by two or more linked points or an example

functions.name: manage the conversation
functions.counts: clarifies, rephrases, checks understanding, or steers the topic on purpose
